title: How xomtra reads your home
desc: Statistics designed for homes: how xomtra turns Home Assistant history into findings you can trust, what it tests before every release and where its limits are.
lead: Every night xomtra goes through the history of your home and finds what is related, what was unusual and what has changed for good. Not with fixed limits per sensor, but with statistics that know how many coincidences the everyday running of a home produces.

pipe.cap: From Home Assistant to an answer

anom.cap: Unusual for this time of the week

sections.h: Any change, from the first day
b: xomtra signs in to Home Assistant with its own read only account. It records every state change the moment it happens and stores the long-term statistics Home Assistant already computes. On the first start it takes over the history Home Assistant still keeps, and after a lost connection it fills in the missing stretch by itself.
Entities that should not be analysed get a label in Home Assistant. Another label keeps them out of storage too.

sections.h: Years of history, in a data lake of its own
b: The data are stored in a data lake on your own disk: compressed column files with a small catalog (DuckLake). Your Home Assistant database stays unchanged and does not grow, and the history can reach back years, not just days.
Every suitable entity becomes one hourly series: the hourly average for measurements, the hourly consumption for meters, and for switches and binary sensors the share of the hour they were on.

Most of what happens in a home follows the time of day and the weather. So xomtra first filters out the daily and weekly rhythm, the effect of the outside temperature and slow trends. What is left is what neither the time of day nor the weather explains, and that is where it starts to get interesting.

sections.h: What is related, and not by chance
b: xomtra compares every pair of series, also shifted by a few hours: the heating switches on and the room warms up later. With hundreds of sensors that means tens of thousands of pairs, and some of them look related by pure chance.
So xomtra learns from your own data how strong a relation chance alone can produce, and it keeps the share of false findings in check across all pairs together, not for each pair separately.

Then it explains what can be explained: sensors in one room, the presence of the residents, a third sensor in between, a hidden common cause, or one quantity measured twice. Such relations are real but say nothing new, so they are ranked after the others. The surprising findings stay at the top.

b.note: A correlation shows where to look, but it does not prove a cause. xomtra says so, and so does your AI assistant.

sections.h: What is unusual in your home
b: A TV running on Saturday evening is normal; at three in the morning on a Tuesday it is not. xomtra compares each series with what is usual in your history for the same time of the week. Appliances that are idle most of the time are judged by their ordinary use, not by their noise at rest.

Unusual times form episodes. An episode is reported only when it is rare compared with all your series together. A separate check looks for lasting changes, such as a fridge that now uses more every day. Episodes during unusual weather, one-hour blips and the period right after a lasting change are marked, so they do not bury the other findings.

sections.h: The surprising first, a summary every Monday
b: Every finding gets a strength, a weight of evidence and a category from a public rulebook: fault, savings, automation or behaviour. Trivial findings, such as the known link between solar power and sunshine, stay hidden.

On Monday morning xomtra saves an overview of the past week, so you can ask what is new, what is gone and what was unusual. Your AI assistant reads the findings over MCP with the same read only rights as any other question and translates them into plain language.

sections.h: Honest about what it does not know
b: A small home, or one where many entities have no area assigned, gives the analysis less to work with. Instead of quietly guessing, xomtra marks such a run as low confidence and presents its relations as hypotheses. Areas in Home Assistant and a presence entity for the residents give it the context it needs.

Analysing a long period over many sensors takes a lot of memory. For a large installation with hundreds of sensors we therefore recommend a machine of its own rather than the add-on on a small Home Assistant host.

sections.h: Tested by the scientific method, with public hypotheses, results and conclusions
b: Any change to the analyses is verified by measurement before a release:

ul: Synthetic homes with a known truth, on every code change: simulated weather, residents, rooms and appliances, relations of known strength and delay, unrelated sensors and the defects real sensors have.

Public data of real homes, every night: series from different homes cannot be related, so every relation found between them is a false one. Artificially planted episodes show how many anomalies xomtra finds.

b: We publish the results as they are, including what is not good enough yet. False relations between different homes are rare in public data, and xomtra finds strong direct relations in synthetic homes. Small homes, homes without areas and people moving around without a presence entity still give more false relations than the target, and part of the moderate anomalies go undetected. The next test is whether people find the findings useful: its procedure is published in advance, the ratings have not been collected yet.
Every number, the runs that measured it and the criteria a release has to meet are in the evaluation document on GitHub.
